paras: The lynching of Bill Reams and Sam Price was the hanging of two jail prisoners, Reams, a Black man, and Price, a white man, by a mob at Clinton, Kentucky, on the night of February 27, 1888. Reams was accused of fatally shooting a man named Jackson who caught him stealing chickens, and Price of killing Hickman County sheriff Henry Winter. Wire reports carried the double lynching nationally, and a later dispatch drew notice by reporting that Price revived after being cut down and was hanged again.

According to a Cairo, Illinois, dispatch, Sheriff Winter had arrested Price near his Clinton home about three months earlier, and Price shot him with a rifle from the doorway of his mother's house. The same account said his mother applauded the shooting and that Price, captured at Dresden, Tennessee, after a $1,200 reward was offered, was held there for a time for fear of lynching at Clinton.

Two nights before the lynching, Jackson was shot twice in the breast by a man reported to be stealing chickens from his yard. The Courier-Journal's Clinton correspondent wrote that Jackson died at 6 o'clock Sunday morning after identifying his attacker as "one Remus, a worthless negro." The Hickman Courier said Reams, "a notoriously bad and dangerous negro," was arrested the next day and identified by Jackson.

Between midnight and 1 a.m., according to the Clinton correspondent, 70 or 80 men surrounded the jail and demanded the keys; the Hickman Courier counted 40 or 50, the wire fifty. The jailer refused, and the county judge, county attorney and sheriff urged the men to let the law take its course, but the mob threatened to blow up the jail, the guards would not fire, and the officers gave up the prisoners. Both were hanged from a tree, at a brickyard in the eastern part of town by the Courier-Journal's account, a sycamore by the wire's. The men, said to be residents of Hickman County, acted in silence on a leader's signal.

The mob also broke open the cell of Price's mother and threatened her with the rope before releasing her. Captain John Cox of Ballard County later reported that Price, cut down by the county judge after the mob left, regained consciousness and spoke. The mob's leaders returned about daylight and hanged him again, two men hanging on his feet until his neck broke; Reams was said to have died almost at once. The authorities cut the bodies down after daylight; Price's was given to his relatives and Reams was buried.

One printing of the Cairo wire said some of the mob had been recognized but that arrests were unlikely. Another wire version said the lynchers "seem to be supported by the people." No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The first report, a brief Cairo dispatch of February 28, ran the next day in the Richmond Dispatch, the Omaha Daily Bee and the Indiana State Sentinel and was reprinted into mid-March. Headlines treated both men's guilt as settled: the Bee's "Two Murderers Lynched" called Reams "a colored chicken thief," and the Macon Beacon ran "Two Assassins Swing Off Quietly."
The re-hanging became a story of its own, run by the New York Sun as "Hanged Him Twice" and reprinted in Ohio, Mississippi and West Virginia, two papers placing Clinton in Illinois.

Closest to the scene, the Hickman Courier headlined "Lynch Law at Clinton" and found "ample justification" for citizens punishing "the murderers." While granting it was "not proper to justify mob law," the paper predicted lynch law would be accepted "as a part of the unwritten law of the land" so long as murders went unpunished. The Courier-Journal's correspondent contrasted Jackson, "a worthy citizen," with Reams, "a worthless negro."

The Hickman Courier and the Clinton correspondent placed the lynching on Monday night; the wire gave 2 o'clock Monday morning and the Cox report Tuesday night. Jackson was variously a farmer, a restaurant keeper and "a worthy citizen," with initials J. P., J. M. or J. H., and was said to have died within hours, at 6 a.m. Sunday, or the next day.

framing.detail: The Hickman Courier headlined 'Lynch Law at Clinton. Two Murderers Hung by the Citizens' and found 'ample justification' for the citizens.
Brief wire items ran under 'Two Men Lynched' and 'Two Murderers Lynched', calling Reams 'a colored chicken thief'.
The Courier-Journal's Clinton dispatch called Jackson 'a worthy citizen' and Reams 'a worthless negro', said the guards sympathized with the mob, and reported the officials' resistance.
The Sun ran the re-hanging as a sensation under 'Hanged Him Twice'; the Evening Star headed its account 'A Kentucky Mob Takes the Law Into Its Own Hands'.
A Chicago News paragraph reprinted in Tallahassee used an 'Illinois' lynching of a negro to answer northern criticism of the South.
